title: Babar Azam Enters Record Books With 2,000 WTC Runs as Captain
excerpt: The Pakistan captain's 76 at Edgbaston made him the fourth batter — and second Asian — to reach 2,000 World Test Championship runs as captain, a milestone that eluded India's Kohli and Rohit. But England completed a 3-0 whitewash.
body:
• Babar Azam became only the fourth batter to score 2,000 runs as captain in the World Test Championship, reaching the mark in 41 innings during Pakistan's second innings at Edgbaston.
  • His 76 off 103 balls was Pakistan's highest score of a fighting 449, which set England a 130-run target on day three of the final Test.
  • He joins Joe Root, Ben Stokes and Dimuth Karunaratne on the elite list — a milestone that eluded India greats Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma as captains.
  • The feat did little to change the match's course: England chased down 130 for the loss of two wickets to complete a 3-0 series whitewash.

Milestone Amid the Wreckage

For two days at Edgbaston, Babar Azam had been a passenger in Pakistan's third Test collapse against England. On Friday, he finally announced his presence — and in doing so, etched his name into the record books. The Pakistan captain struck a fluent 76 off 103 balls, the innings that carried him past 2,000 runs as captain in the World Test Championship, making him only the fourth batter in history to reach the landmark in the tournament's five-year existence.

Babar got there in 41 innings, the third-fastest to the milestone. Joe Root and Dimuth Karunaratne share the record of reaching it in 40 innings each, while Ben Stokes required 61. The all-time list now reads: Root (3,060 runs in 66 innings), Stokes (2,182 in 71), Karunaratne (2,160 in 45) and Babar (2,015 in 41). Kraigg Brathwaite of the West Indies, with 1,994 runs in 64 innings, is next in line.

Perhaps the most striking detail for followers of the subcontinent's cricket rivalry: Babar is only the second Asian batter to reach 2,000 WTC runs as captain, after Karunaratne. Two of India's greatest modern batters never got close — Virat Kohli tallied 1,349 runs in 37 innings as captain in the WTC, and Rohit Sharma 1,254.

Pakistan's Fightback Falls Short

Babar's innings, which included 11 fours and a six off Jofra Archer, was his first half-century of the three-Test series. He had missed the opening Test through injury and arrived at Edgbaston under mounting scrutiny — his vulnerability to the short ball was brutally exposed earlier in the series, with Archer's bouncer dismissals in particular drawing pointed commentary about the gap between his white-ball pedigree and his Test returns.

Friday's effort briefly suggested a response. Walking in at 125 for three, Babar looked comfortable for the first time in the series, steering Pakistan toward a total of 449. Shan Masood led the resistance with a determined 95, opener Azan Awais made 59, and the pair's 125-run third-wicket stand was Pakistan's first century partnership of the entire tour. The 129-run lead left England needing 130 for victory on day four.

It was not enough. England, who had already sealed the series with crushing wins — an innings and 103 runs in the first Test and 194 runs in the second — chased down the target with two wickets down to complete the 3-0 whitewash. Babar's dismissal, caught fine off Josh Tongue after England reprised their short-ball plan, continued his Test century drought and meant the record came in another losing cause.

What the Numbers Say About Babar's Captaincy Era

Personal milestones during a series whitewash invite a familiar debate, and this tour has sharpened it. Pakistan won just one Test away from home in the three years preceding this series — against the West Indies last month — and the chaos around the squad has been unmistakable: seven players were sent home after the second Test defeat at Lord's, with coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul sacked in the aftermath.

Babar's individual record as leader remains impressive on paper. His 41-innings path to 2,000 WTC runs as captain puts him ahead of Stokes (61) and Brathwaite (64), and alongside Misbah-ul-Haq he is one of only two Pakistan captains to cross 7,000 runs in international cricket. At 31, he is the youngest of the five Pakistan captains to reach 2,000 Test runs in the role. The counterpoint is that none of those numbers have translated into sustained Test success for the side, and his first-innings dismissal at Edgbaston — bowled by Tongue for seven — was as symptomatic of Pakistan's problems as anything in the series.

What's Next

For Pakistan, the whitewash completes a demoralising tour and leaves the team management — what remains of it — with hard questions before the next WTC cycle fixtures. For Babar, the milestone confirms his statistical standing among the greats of the format's modern era, even as the search for a defining Test-series victory as captain continues. England, meanwhile, march on with a pace attack — Tongue, Archer, Ollie Robinson — that looks increasingly formidable in home conditions.
